council-waterfront-vote.title: A Waterfront Vote Splits a City Council That Used to Agree on Everything
council-waterfront-vote.dek: In Port Ellery, a plan to replace a working pier with housing has turned a sleepy council into a nightly argument.
body: PORT ELLERY, Conn. - For eleven years the seven members of this city's council voted together so reliably that the local paper stopped printing the tallies. That ended in January, when a developer's proposal to replace Pier 4 with three hundred apartments came before them and the vote was 4 to 3.

The pier is the last in the harbor still used by commercial fishing boats, and the boats are the reason a quarter of the city's restaurants exist. But the pier also needs eleven million dollars of repairs the city does not have, and the housing plan would pay for a new, smaller landing at the far end of the harbor.

'Everyone in this room wants both things,' said Councilwoman Renata Osei, who voted against the plan. 'We want the boats and we want the apartments. What we disagree about is which one we can afford to lose if the other one does not work out.'

The council has met four times since the vote to consider amendments. The most recent session ran past midnight and ended with a motion to hire an independent engineer to price the repairs, which passed 7 to 0. It was, several members noted afterward, the first unanimous vote of the year.
The developer, Ellery Landing Partners, has said it will withdraw the proposal if the council does not approve a final plan by June. A public meeting is scheduled for March 19.

links.label: Opinion: the case for keeping Pier 4

comments.author: harborwatch
comments.text: The engineer study is the only sensible thing that has happened in this whole process.

opinion-keep-the-pier.title: Port Ellery Should Keep Its Pier, and Build the Apartments Anyway
opinion-keep-the-pier.dek: The council is being asked to choose between a harbor and a housing plan. It is a false choice.
body: I grew up three streets from Pier 4, and I have watched the same argument recur every decade of my life: the harbor is expensive, the land is valuable, and someone has a plan. What is new this time is that the plan is good. Three hundred apartments in a city that has built nine in five years is not a small thing.

But the plan's authors have made a category error. They have treated the pier as a cost and the apartments as a revenue, when the pier is what makes the apartments worth building. Nobody is paying a premium to look at a parking structure.

The engineer the council just hired will, I suspect, find that the pier's repairs can be phased, and that a smaller housing footprint on the upland lot could fund the first phase without touching the landing at all. That plan exists. It was drawn in 2017 and shelved because it was less profitable, not because it was worse.
The council should ask for it back. The news story on the vote is at http://nytimes.com/2026/council-waterfront-vote

trade-pact-textiles.title: A Textile Deal Between Two Small Countries Is Rattling a Very Large Industry
trade-pact-textiles.dek: Calderra and Sunwick have agreed to drop tariffs on finished garments. Buyers in three continents are redrawing their supply maps.
body: The agreement signed in Sunwick's capital last week runs to nineteen pages and covers a single category of goods. Its effect on the apparel trade has been out of all proportion to its length.

Calderra grows cotton and spins it; Sunwick, an hour's flight away, has the sewing capacity and a port. For thirty years a tariff on finished garments crossing between them meant the cloth went by sea to a third country to be cut and stitched. From July, it will not have to.

Buyers for large retailers, who had assumed the third-country route was permanent, are now pricing the direct one. 'It takes eleven days out of the lead time,' said one sourcing director, who asked not to be named because her employer had not announced its plans. 'Eleven days is a whole season's worth of decisions.'

Officials in the country that had been doing the stitching declined to comment. Analysts expect it to seek a similar arrangement with Calderra within the year, which would put the three economies back roughly where they started, with one fewer ocean crossing in the middle.
The pact takes effect on July 1. A companion agreement on yarn is under negotiation.

comments.author: sourcing_pat
comments.text: The eleven days is the whole story. Everything else is downstream of that.

gridline-antitrust-suit.title: States Sue Gridline, Saying Its Calendar App Boxed Out Rivals
gridline-antitrust-suit.dek: Fourteen attorneys general say the software giant tied its scheduling tool to its email service in a way that made competing products unusable.
body: A coalition of fourteen states filed suit against Gridline Software on Monday, accusing the company of using its dominant email product to disadvantage rival calendar applications. The complaint, filed in federal court in Delaware, says Gridline degraded the way invitations from outside calendars appeared in its inbox while showing its own invitations in full.

Gridline, which says its email service has four hundred million active accounts, called the suit 'a misreading of a security feature' and said the differences in display were designed to warn users about invitations from unverified senders.

The suit relies heavily on internal messages obtained through a prior investigation, including one in which a product manager wrote that the display change would 'make Tessera look broken.' Tessera, a calendar startup, closed in 2024 after its user numbers fell by half in a year.

'This is not a case about a company building a better product,' said the attorney general leading the coalition. 'It is a case about a company deciding that the way to win was to make everyone else's product look worse.'

Legal scholars said the case would turn on whether Gridline's email service counts as a market of its own. Gridline's lawyers have argued in earlier matters that email is one feature of a broader productivity suite in which the company faces vigorous competition.
A hearing on the states' request for a preliminary injunction is scheduled for April.

links.label: Opinion: the Gridline suit is about defaults

comments.author: tessera_alum
comments.text: I worked there. We spent the last eight months of the company trying to figure out why our invites rendered as plain text. Now I know.

opinion-defaults-are-the-product.title: The Gridline Case Is Really About Who Owns the Default
opinion-defaults-are-the-product.dek: Antitrust law was written for railroads and oil. It is being asked to reason about a drop-down menu.
body: The fourteen states suing Gridline have a strong story and a weak precedent. The story is that Gridline made a rival's product look broken. The precedent problem is that no court has ever been asked to say what a company owes the products that live inside its own inbox.

The honest answer is that the inbox is infrastructure now. Four hundred million people route their working lives through it, and a change to how it renders an invitation is closer to a change in a building code than to a change in a product. We regulate building codes. We hold hearings.

Gridline will say that treating its inbox as infrastructure would freeze it in place, and there is something to that. But the alternative, in which a company may quietly break the products of anyone who competes with it, is not a market. It is a landlord.
The news report is at http://nytimes.com/2026/gridline-antitrust-suit

deep-vent-microbes.title: In a Vent Two Miles Down, Microbes That Eat Rust and Make Something Stranger
deep-vent-microbes.dek: A research cruise off the Kestrel Ridge has found a community of organisms that appear to run on iron alone.
body: The vent field is not large, perhaps the size of a tennis court, and it was found by accident when a survey vehicle strayed off its planned track. What it contained has kept a shipboard laboratory awake for most of a month.

The microbes coating the vent chimneys draw their energy from oxidizing iron, which is not itself unusual. What is unusual is the by-product. Instead of the rust crusts that iron-eating microbes usually leave behind, these produce a fine, layered mineral that the team has not yet been able to match to any known species of the material.

'We have a sample in a vial that should not exist according to the textbook,' said Dr. Ilse Brandt, the cruise's chief scientist, speaking by satellite phone. 'Either the textbook is incomplete, which is likely, or we have contaminated the vial, which we have checked five times.'
Samples are being flown to three laboratories for independent analysis. The team has not named the organism and says it will not until the mineral is identified.
The ridge lies in international waters. A second cruise is planned for the autumn.

restaurant-review-larkspur.title: Review: At Larkspur, a Chef Cooks the Meal She Wanted at Twenty-Two
restaurant-review-larkspur.dek: A twenty-eight-seat room in a former hardware store serves the most confident food in the city right now. Three stars.
body: The room at Larkspur still has the hardware store's shelving, and on the night I visited a shelf that once held paint held instead a row of jars of preserved lemons, each dated in marker. It is that kind of place: the details are real and none of them are for you.

Chef Simone Achebe, who is thirty-four and opened Larkspur last September after eight years in other people's kitchens, has said the menu is the meal she wished someone had cooked for her at twenty-two, when she was broke and hungry and eating well was the only luxury she could imagine. It shows. The food is generous in a way that has gone out of fashion.

A plate of roasted carrots arrives under a blanket of brown butter and toasted buckwheat and is, absurdly, the best thing on a menu that also includes a whole braised lamb shoulder for two. The shoulder is very good. The carrots are something else.
Service is warm and slightly chaotic, and the wine list is short and fairly priced. Dessert is a single option each night, take it or leave it. Take it.
Larkspur, 114 Fenwick Street. Dinner Wednesday through Sunday. Reservations released a month ahead and gone within the hour.

links.label: Cooking: the brown-butter carrots, at home

cooking-brown-butter-carrots.title: Roasted Carrots With Brown Butter and Buckwheat
cooking-brown-butter-carrots.dek: The dish everyone leaves Larkspur talking about is, it turns out, four ingredients and forty minutes.
body: Simone Achebe was reluctant to give up this recipe, not because it is secret but because, she said, 'people will see how simple it is and think I am cheating.' She is not cheating. The dish depends on carrots roasted hard enough to blister and butter browned further than most people dare.

Heat the oven to 450 degrees. Scrub two pounds of medium carrots, halve them lengthwise, toss with two tablespoons of olive oil and a teaspoon of salt, and roast cut side down on a sheet pan for thirty to thirty-five minutes, until the undersides are dark and the tips have charred.

While they roast, toast a quarter cup of buckwheat groats in a dry pan until they smell nutty, then set aside. In the same pan, melt six tablespoons of butter over medium heat and keep cooking, swirling, until the solids are the color of a hazelnut shell and it smells almost burnt. Pull it at once.
Pile the carrots on a platter, pour the butter over, scatter the buckwheat, and finish with flaky salt and a squeeze of lemon. Serves four as a side, or two people who have decided this is dinner.
The review of Larkspur is at http://nytimes.com/2026/restaurant-review-larkspur

valmora-strait-summit.title: Three Nations, One Strait and a Fee Schedule Nobody Can Agree On
valmora-strait-summit.dek: The Meridian Strait talks in Valmora were supposed to take a day. They are in their fifth.
body: VALMORA - The delegations arrived on Monday with a draft they had agreed in principle in December, and by Tuesday evening the principle had come apart over a single column of a table on page twelve: who collects the pilotage fee, and how much of it they keep.

The Meridian Strait is eleven miles wide at its narrowest and carries a tenth of the region's tanker traffic. All three coastal states supply pilots; none wants to be the one that supplies them for free.

The smallest delegation, from Isle Corvane, has argued that its coast guard does most of the rescue work in the strait and should receive the largest share. The two larger states have offered a formula based on the length of coastline, which happens to favor them.
Diplomats on all sides say the deal will be done. 'Nobody is going home without a signature,' said one. 'The question is how many more dinners we have to sit through first.'
A joint statement is expected Friday.

harbourside-surge-aftermath.title: After the Surge, Harbourside Asks Why a 2019 Report Went Unread
harbourside-surge-aftermath.dek: A review that recommended raising the sea barrier by a meter was filed, acknowledged and never funded.
body: The report is forty pages long, and its central recommendation appears on page three: the Harbourside barrier, built in 1974, should be raised by one meter before 2025 to account for the sea level and storm patterns the authors expected by then. The council received it in November 2019 and voted to 'note' it.
On Saturday the sea came over the barrier by roughly sixty centimeters. Two thousand people were evacuated, and most are still in school gyms and hotels while their ground floors dry.

The council leader, who was not in office in 2019, said the report would now be implemented in full. Residents at a meeting on Monday evening were less interested in the future than in the word 'note.'
'Noted means nothing,' said Amos Ferreira, who has run a chandlery on the front for thirty years and lost most of his stock. 'I want to know who read it and decided it could wait.'
The damage estimate is expected in two weeks.

orchestra-strike-settlement.title: The Meridian Philharmonic Settles a Nine-Week Strike, and Plays That Night
orchestra-strike-settlement.dek: Musicians accepted a contract that ties raises to ticket revenue. The first concert back sold out in an afternoon.
body: The musicians ratified the contract at four in the afternoon and were on stage by eight. The program, changed at the last minute, opened with a fanfare that the orchestra's principal trumpet said she had chosen 'because it is loud, and we have been quiet for nine weeks.'

The strike, the orchestra's first in a generation, turned on a proposal to freeze base salaries for three years. The settlement instead links annual raises to the previous season's ticket revenue, with a floor of two percent and a ceiling of six.
Management called the formula 'a shared bet on the audience.' The musicians' negotiating committee called it 'a way to find out whether the board believes its own marketing.'
The remaining season has been reorganized to make up eleven of the fourteen cancelled concerts. Subscribers will be offered the three missing dates as credit.

bakery-chain-ipo.title: A Bakery Chain That Refused to Franchise Is Going Public Instead
bakery-chain-ipo.dek: Hearthline has two hundred company-owned stores and a founder who says the offering is 'the least bad way to open the next two hundred.'
body: Hearthline Bakeries filed for an initial public offering on Tuesday, seeking to raise about three hundred million dollars for a company that has, for nineteen years, grown only as fast as its own cash would allow.

The founder, Mireille Dubois, has been public about her dislike of franchising, which she says produces 'two hundred versions of a store and none of them mine.' The filing preserves that stance: every store will remain company-owned, and the proceeds will fund a commissary network and two hundred new locations over five years.

The filing shows revenue of four hundred and twenty million dollars last year and a small profit. Analysts said the valuation the company is seeking, roughly two billion dollars, prices in a growth rate it has never before attempted.
'She is betting that the thing that made the stores good survives being done twice as fast,' said one analyst. 'It might. It usually does not.'

replay-tools-enterprise.title: Why Big Companies Are Suddenly Paying for Software That Runs Slower
replay-tools-enterprise.dek: Deterministic simulators trade speed for the ability to replay a failure exactly. Enterprise buyers have decided the trade is worth it.
body: For most of the history of computing, the pitch for a new tool has been that it is faster. A small category of software is now selling itself on the opposite claim: it is slower, on purpose, and in exchange it will show you exactly what went wrong.

Enterprise buyers, particularly in finance and infrastructure, have been the earliest adopters. 'We spend more on finding bugs than on fixing them,' said the head of platform engineering at a large payments company. 'Anything that turns finding into a mechanical step pays for itself in a quarter.'

The trade-off is real. Simulated runs are typically several times slower than native ones, and the tools do not help with failures that only appear at full speed. Vendors say that category is smaller than engineers assume.

opinion-slow-cities.title: The Cities That Are Winning Are the Ones That Stopped Hurrying
opinion-slow-cities.dek: Port Ellery took four meetings to hire an engineer. That is not dysfunction. That is government.
body: There is a fashionable idea that the problem with local government is speed, and that if councils only moved faster, more would get built. I have covered councils for twenty years and I have never seen a bad decision improved by making it sooner.

The councils I have watched succeed share one trait: they are willing to spend a meeting doing nothing but establishing what is true. It is boring. It produces no headlines. It is also the only reliable way to keep from voting on a fiction.
Speed is a virtue in a kitchen and a fire station. In a council chamber it is mostly a way of making sure the argument happens after the vote instead of before it.
